title: Nanoscale mapping of native defects in Td-MoTe2 and their impact on graphene-based van der Waals heterostructures
authors: Wojciech Ryś, Iaroslav Lutsyk, Mindaugas Lukosius, Przemysław Przybysz, Paweł Dąbrowski, Maciej Rogala, Paweł Krukowski, Paweł J. Kowalczyk
abstract: We investigate native defects and their impact on the electronic structure of Td-MoTe2 and graphene/Td-MoTe2 van der Waals heterostructures using scanning tunnelling microscopy and spectroscopy. STM reveals a high density of circular, hollow surface defects that we attribute to Te vacancies. STS on pristine MoTe2 shows semimetallic, V-shaped dI/dV spectra with subtle low-energy states. The vacancies suppress the tunnelling conductance below the Fermi level without introducing new sharp defect-related resonances, consistent with a vacancy-induced redistribution of Mo-Te spectral weight rather than the appearance of new electronic states. In the heterostructure, graphene preserves these MoTe2 fingerprints with no noticeable graphene doping or charge transfer. Our results demonstrate that isolated native Te vacancies act as spectroscopically weak perturbations to the low-energy electronic structure of graphene. The graphene overlayer further screens their impact on the electronic structure, making graphene/Td-MoTe2 heterostructures intrinsically tolerant to such interface defects.
summary: This work uses STM and STS to map native Te vacancies in Td-MoTe2 and analyze their electronic impact on graphene/MoTe2 heterostructures. The findings show that while vacancies perturb the electronic structure, the overlying graphene layer significantly screens these defects. This suggests that such heterostructures are robust and potentially defect-tolerant for device applications.
main_problem: The study investigates how native defects, specifically Te vacancies, affect the electronic structure of Td-MoTe2 and how this interaction is modified when graphene is overlaid to form a van der Waals heterostructure.
main_result: Isolated Te vacancies cause spectroscopically weak perturbations to the low-energy electronic structure of graphene, and the graphene overlayer effectively screens the impact of these interface defects, making the heterostructure intrinsically tolerant.
method: The research employed Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM) for topography and Scanning Tunneling Spectroscopy (STS) to probe the local electronic density of states.
model_or_system: The physical system is the Td-MoTe2 transition metal dichalcogenide interfaced with graphene, forming a van der Waals heterostructure. Defects are identified as Te vacancies.
key_observables: dI/dV spectra (tunneling conductance), STM topography (hollow circular sites), and the persistence of MoTe2 electronic 'fingerprints' in the heterostructure.
important_parameters: Defect density ($\sim 0.03 - 0.04 	ext{ per nm}^2$), temperature (77 K), and bias voltage ranges (e.g., below -0.1 V vs. -0.3 V).
main_assumptions: The suppression of conductance is interpreted as a redistribution of Mo–Te spectral weight rather than the introduction of new, sharp electronic states.
figures_summary: Figures show STM topographies comparing pristine and defective areas, and STS data (dI/dV curves and maps) comparing measurements on bare MoTe2 versus the graphene/MoTe2 heterostructure across different defect conditions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first characterizing the material and identifying Te vacancies via STM, then using STS to quantify the electronic impact of these vacancies on pristine MoTe2, and finally demonstrating the mitigating effect of the graphene overlayer on the defect signatures.
why_interesting: While primarily condensed matter/materials science, the study of defect-induced electronic perturbations and the screening effect by an overlying 2D material (graphene) is highly relevant to understanding interface engineering in quantum devices and open quantum systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1. a) Ball-and-stick side-view model of graphene/MoTe2 heterostructure. Black, blue, and yellow balls correspond to carbon, molybdenum, and tellurium, respectively. b) A high-resolution STM topography of the UHV- exfoliated Td-MoTe2 (I = 0.3 nA; U = 0.15 V). c) The exemplary surface of graphene/MoTe2 (I = 0.2 nA; V = 0.35 V). The FFT and close-up surface images are shown in the insets. The graphene and TMDC surface unit cells are again marked by violet and red shapes, respectively. All data were acquired at ~77 K and FFT-filtered.

Figure 2. The images show a set of representative defect topographies for the pristine and hybrid MoTe2 systems. a) Typical pristine surface point-like defects for Td-MoTe2 surface (I = 0.7 nA; U = 0.07 V). b) Round, hollow defects present in the graphene/Td-MoTe2 system (I = 0.05 nA, U = -0.6 V). c) The depth profiles measured along the arrows drawn in “b”. All measurements were acquired at ~77 K. All the images shown are FFT-filtered.

Figure 1. The set of histograms depicting the occurrence rates of the STS peak maxima for each acquired STS map. a) Data acquired for the pristine MoTe2. b) Data acquired for the MoTe2 defect sites. c) Data acquired for the defect-free surface of the heterostructure. d) Data acquired for the defect sites on the heterostructure. The intensities of the curves in each quadrant are normalised to facilitate comparison.

Figure 2. The flattened STS maps. The spectra originate from all the cross-section dI/dV maps present in the work and in the supplementary information. a) Pristine Td-MoTe2 map from Fig. 3c. b) Td-MoTe2 defect map from Fig. S3b. c) Heterostructure map from Fig. 3f. More details can be found in the methods section of the main text.

Figure 3. The STS data sets acquired for a typical defect in Td-MoTe2. a) A selection of dI/dV data slices (5×12 nm in size), b) the dI/dV data averaged along the profile drawn in a and b, c) the STS curves corresponding to the slices taken along the cuts of the profile in a. There is a min/max contour added to the curves, which corresponds to the thinner averaged profiles to highlight the volatility range. The spectra were acquired at ~80 K (I = 0.4 nA; U = -0.08 V).
